extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and researchers interested in literary hoaxes, authorial identity, and contemporary literature
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedia article describing the creation, publications, public exposure, legal aftermath, and cultural reception of a literary persona (JT LeRoy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: This section needs additional citations for verification. Please help improve this article by adding citations to reliable sources. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikipedia editorial standard: substantive claims should be supported by reliable sources; material lacking citations is subject to challenge or removal. Authors/editors should add inline references to trustworthy publications to verify claims in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of authorship / author identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The authenticity of LeRoy has been a subject of debate, even as details of the creation came to light in the 2000s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating works presented as semi‑autobiographical or authored by a claimed persona requires scrutiny of authorial provenance; revelations about true authorship can change critical and public reception and may trigger investigative journalism, legal action, memoirs, and documentary treatments (examples on page: New York magazine exposé, New York Times reporting, Savannah Knoop memoir, documentaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and ethics of pseudonyms / alter egos
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeremiah Terminator LeRoy is a literary persona created by Laura Albert; Albert described LeRoy as her 'veil'. The article notes that the concept of an alter ego is longstanding (e.g., Mary Shelley) and discusses both critique and defense of Albert's actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or producing work under a pseudonym or persona, consider historical precedent, artistic intent, ethical implications (deception vs. privacy/protection), potential reputational consequences, and legal risks (e.g., fraud lawsuits). The page documents both critical condemnation and defenses arguing for the artistic legitimacy of alter egos.
